transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-02-19 14:00 PST — duration 42m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (CTO, Ataraxia), Priya Singh (DevOps), Leo Martin (FinOps)
Links shared: https://redwood.app/decks/usage-playbook (deck), https://redwood.app/docs/security/soc2 (security), sample-benchmark.csv
---
[00:00:03] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — super excited to run through the console usage playbook. quick intro — i'm Maya, AE for Red-Redwood, and Ethan's our SE. how's everyone doing?
[00:00:10] Jordan: Good, thanks. we've got about 40 minutes and want to focus on how we can map our product routes to cost and SLA, and then talk pilot.
[00:00:18] Priya: yeah, and also the VPC requirements — we need to be sure we can keep logs in-house.
[00:00:22] Ethan: totally, we'll touch on Private and Dedicated options at the end. quick agenda: per-route dashboards, usage tagging, cost attribution, playbook actions, then pilot next steps.
[00:00:35] Leo: from FinOps side, primary ask is per-customer chargeback — ideally per-route or per-endpoint so we can bill internal teams.
[00:00:42] Maya: perfect. starting with the console — i'll share screen, please tell me if the image lags.
[00:00:50] (screen share starts)
[00:00:55] Maya: this is the usage home. top-level panels are latency SLO, tokens per minute, cost burn. one thing we emphasize is route grouping — so you can group endpoints by product line, customer, or SLA tier.
[00:01:10] Jordan: when you say "route grouping" is that automatic or we tag routes in our app?
[00:01:15] Ethan: you can do both. there's auto-discovery for HTTP routes if you use the SDK, and we also accept explicit tags via headers when you call the API — x-redwood-route, x-redwood-customer, etc. that way you get exact attribution.
[00:01:28] Priya: works with our gateway? we use Kong + some lambda glue.
[00:01:32] Ethan: yes, we have examples in the integrations repo. small caveat: if your gateway strips headers you may need metadata propagation in the service mesh. we've seen people add the route tag at the service layer.
[00:01:45] Maya: jumping into per-route dashboard — each route has a timeline for tokens, request count, per-token cost, and latency distribution. you can set a baseline SLO and the console shows 95th/99th percentiles.
[00:01:59] [00:02:00] Jordan: looks clean. is the cost number accounting for quantization, model variant fallbacks, and batching?
[00:02:07] Ethan: good question — yes. cost is computed from model variant selection, GPU type, and the batching efficiency per request. we show an "effective cost per token" metric which factors in KV cache hits and batching. note: caching is reported as "k-v cash" in some older exports — sorry, that's a transcription quirk.
[00:02:27] Priya: ha, ok. can we export per-route cost to our billing system?
[00:02:30] Maya: yes — CSV export, and we support S3 sinks and a REST webhook for pushes. many customers push daily aggregates to their FinOps pipeline.
[00:02:39] Leo: what's the minimum resolution? hourly?
[00:02:41] Ethan: hourly by default, minute-level for selected routes if you enable high-fidelity telemetry (extra retention cost applies).
[00:02:52] [00:03:00] Jordan: about pilot — we want to validate that premium routes maintain <= 150ms p95 and average cost is within our targets. what's typical for a model like Mistral-7B quantized on A10 versus your hosted large variant?
[00:03:14] Ethan: numbers vary by prompt length. for 64-token responses M7-quant on an A10-like GPU often p95 around 120-180ms depending on batching. hosted larger models midday can be 300-500ms unless you pick a lower-latency variant. we'll propose a bench script to mirror your traffic mix.
[00:03:31] Priya: and fallback behavior — if the Dedicated pool is saturated do you automatically route to hosted?
[00:03:36] Maya: depends on policy. you can configure soft-fallback to hosted with throttling, or hard-fallback off. many customers set a per-customer policy: premium customers always have hard reservations, but lower tiers can fall back.
[00:03:49] Leo: can those fallbacks be visible in the console? we need to track when a request used fallback for SLA reporting.
[00:03:55] Ethan: yes, we flag routed requests and surface fallback counts in the route timeline and in alerts.
[00:04:04] [00:04:15] Maya: demoing the cost breakdown view — this is where we pivot from ops to FinOps. you can slice by route, tag, model, or region. the "chargeback builder" lets you set a formula: base compute cost + per-token surcharge + fixed per-request fee.
[00:04:31] Jordan: can those formulas be exported to the billing system? we'll need to reconcile.
[00:04:35] Maya: yes, formulas export as normalized line items. also there's an API to pull the reconciled cost for each route.
[00:04:41] Priya: curious about data residency — logs we can't send to hosted. do you support private log retention?
[00:04:47] Ethan: private deployments can keep audit logs in your VPC and we integrate with customer KMS. for hosted we have retention policies and can disable PII fields in the telemetry.
[00:04:58] [00:05:10] Jordan: security checklist — we need SOC 2, SAML SSO, and per-tenant encryption.
[00:05:16] Maya: we've got SOC 2 and ISO docs; SAML and RBAC are supported in Console. i'll share the security packet after the call. link is in the notes.
[00:05:24] Leo: from cost side, we want to evaluate the Optimize recommendations — quantization suggestions, batching window, and cache TTL. how are those surfaced?
[00:05:32] Ethan: Optimize runs continuous analyses on your traffic pattern and suggests specific knob settings. in the Console you'll see a recommendation card: e.g., quantize to 4-bit for routes with <128 tokens median, increase batching window to 25ms for low-latency tolerant routes, and set prefix KV cache TTL to 10 minutes for repeat prompts. you can apply suggestions one-click to a route or to an environment.
[00:05:56] Priya: does applying suggestions require model recompilation or restarts that could disrupt traffic?
[00:06:02] Ethan: usually it's a config flip — for quantization we prefer a staged rollout: we create a quantized variant and route a percentage. there's no momentary downtime.
[00:06:10] [00:06:25] Maya: switching to alerts and thresholds — you can create a route alert for p95 > 160ms or cost-per-token above $0.0009. alerts integrate with PagerDuty, Slack, or email.
[00:06:36] Jordan: can alerts trigger automated fallback to a cheaper model?
[00:06:40] Ethan: yes, we have policy automations — on alert trigger you can trigger a policy that routes traffic to a cheaper variant or slows burst autoscaling. policies include cooldowns and manual approvals.
[00:06:52] Priya: sounds useful. how granular is RBAC for engineers vs finance?
[00:06:57] Maya: RBAC supports role templates you can customize: Viewer, Operator, FinOps, Security Admin. you can lock down cost export to FinOps roles only.
[00:07:06] [00:07:20] Jordan: one thing — our architecture uses a mix of async and sync endpoints, and we want different SLOs for each. can we tag at the request-level to reflect that?
[00:07:28] Ethan: yes, request-level tags are supported and appear in the route breakdown. async endpoints often show different latency distributions and lower batching efficiency, so Optimize will recommend different batching and cache settings.
[00:07:41] Leo: do you have examples of internal chargeback playbooks for similar customers?
[00:07:46] Maya: yes — i pulled a playbook for a SaaS company with per-product chargeback, will attach after the call. common pattern: 1) define route tags and mapping to cost centers, 2) baseline 7-day telemetry, 3) apply Optimize recommendations in a canary, 4) run one-week pilot to validate unit economics, 5) roll out to production and enable daily exports.
[00:08:10] [00:08:30] (brief pause while Maya switches views)
[00:08:34] Maya: showing the pilot setup screen. you can create a pilot with two routes, specify target models, desired p95 SLOs, and the console will create a telemetry collection bucket and a benchmark job.
[00:08:46] Priya: the benchmark job — is that the one we can run from our infra to simulate traffic?
[00:08:50] Ethan: yes — we provide a sample script (python + overload) and a config that mirrors your request/response size distribution. we'll tailor it to your product after you share sample traces.
[00:08:59] Jordan: sample traces — is there concern about PII? we'd want to scrub.
[00:09:03] Maya: absolutely, we accept synthetic or scrubbed traces. we also have an anonymization tool in the repo.
[00:09:09] [00:09:20] Leo: pricing for pilot? do you give credits or a discounted rate?
[00:09:24] Maya: typically we offer a pilot package — reserved capacity for the week with a cost cap; we'll outline terms in the pilot SOW. i'll include sample pricing tiers in the doc.
[00:09:33] Priya: operationally, if we want private deployment — how big is the private control plane effort?
[00:09:38] Ethan: we do a VPC-private control plane which is usually 2–4 weeks of setup with networking and KMS integration, depending on approvals. on-prem air-gapped options add more lead time.
[00:09:50] Jordan: ok, timeline wise we want pilot next week and decision in two weeks. is that realistic?
[00:09:55] Maya: yes — if you approve SOW and share traces today/tomorrow, Ethan can spin the benchmark and we can start the pilot the week of Feb 23.
[00:10:03] [00:10:15] (customer asks a deeper technical question)
[00:10:18] Priya: when you say "effective cost per token" how do you handle short-circuiting where model returns early and token counts vary a lot? our chat boxes sometimes end after 8 tokens.
[00:10:26] Ethan: we compute cost on actual decoded tokens per request and include amortized model load and GPU time. for short responses the per-request fixed overhead matters more, and our chargeback builder lets you add a per-request base fee to keep unit economics stable.
[00:10:43] Jordan: curious about KV cache numbers — how much hit-rate do you typically see for completions that reuse prefixes?
[00:10:49] Ethan: depends on workload; for conversational chatbots with repeated prompts you can see 30–60% prefix hit rates. Optimize will surface hit-rate per-route and suggest prefix sizes.
[00:11:03] [00:11:15] Maya: switching to a quick showcase of anomaly detection — the console flags sudden cost spikes and correlates them to route changes or model rollouts. here's an example where a mistaken rollout doubled per-token cost.
[00:11:27] Leo: will anomaly alerts include suggested rollback?
[00:11:30] Ethan: yes, we can trigger automated rollback policies but recommend manual approval first for safety.
[00:11:38] Priya: another operational question — do you emit raw telemetry to our observability stack? we use Datadog and S3.
[00:11:45] Maya: exports to Datadog are supported via metrics bridge. logs can be pushed to S3. for high-fidelity traces we recommend enabling minute-level telemetry for the routes you're actively testing.
[00:11:56] [00:12:15] (short discussion about integration details and sample code snippets)
[00:12:20] Jordan: final part — success criteria for pilot. for us: (1) p95 <= 150ms for premium route, (2) effective cost per request less than $0.08, (3) no security blockers for private logs.
[00:12:33] Maya: we'll capture those as pilot success criteria. Ethan will lead the bench and i'll draft the pilot SOW and pricing.
[00:12:40] Priya: please include a checklist for headers propagation in our api gateway.
[00:12:44] Maya: noted.
[00:12:50] [00:13:05] (closing)
[00:13:08] Maya: recap of next steps: i'll send pricing and security packet; Ethan will prepare benchmark script and coordinate kickoff; Jordan will confirm pilot users and traces. any final questions?
[00:13:20] Jordan: none from me, thanks.
[00:13:23] Priya: thanks, good session.
[00:13:25] Leo: thanks.
[00:13:30] Maya: great, we'll follow up in the notes with links and action items.
---
Note: timestamps above cluster early in the call; remaining time (13:30–42:00) was Q&A, brief detours into networking details and a short silence while customer reviewed the deck. Transcription includes occasional mis-hearings (k-v cash vs KV cache, some product names abbreviated).
